g9-mathematics-um2-t1.overview: Natural numbers grew into integers, integers into rationals — and then the rationals failed. This topic completes the ladder to the real numbers and shows why √2 broke Pythagoras' world.
objectives: Classify numbers as natural, integer, rational or irrational
Convert between fractions and terminating/recurring decimals
Prove informally that √2 is irrational
Place real numbers on the number line
Compare and order real numbers including surds
g9-mathematics-um2-t1.simple: Every fraction is a decimal that either stops (1/4 = 0.25) or repeats forever in a pattern (1/3 = 0.333…). A number that does neither — decimals that never end AND never repeat, like √2 = 1.41421356… — is irrational. The rationals (fractions) plus the irrationals (√2, π,…) together fill the entire number line: those are the reals. Think of it as a family tree: naturals ⊂ whole numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals joining at the top.
g9-mathematics-um2-t1.detailed:
The natural numbers ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …} count objects; adding 0 gives the whole numbers, and adding negatives gives the integers ℤ. Division forced the next expansion: a rational number is anything writable as a/b with a, b integers, b ≠ 0. Every integer is rational (5 = 5/1), so each system nests inside the next: ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ.

Rationals have a decimal fingerprint: terminate (3/8 = 0.375) or recur with a repeating block (2/11 = 0.181818…). The converse also holds: any terminating or recurring decimal is a fraction, hence rational. Converting 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8; converting a recurring decimal uses a subtraction trick — for x = 0.3̄ (i.e. x = 0.333…), 10x = 3.333…, so 9x = 3 and x = 1/3. Multiply by 10ᵏ where k is the repeat length, subtract, and solve.

Irrational numbers cannot be written as fractions. The classic example is √2. The ancient proof: suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then a² = 2b², so a² is even, so a is even, say a = 2c. Then 4c² = 2b² gives b² = 2c², so b is even too — both a and b even, contradicting 'lowest terms'. No such fraction exists. Similar arguments (and the calculator's non-repeating display) reveal π, e, and √p for prime p as irrational.

The reals ℝ = rationals ∪ irrationals fill the number line completely: every point names a real, and every real names a point. Gaps that remained after ℚ — like the point at distance √2 from 0 — are exactly filled by irrationals. Geometry makes them visible: the diagonal of a unit square has length √2; a circle of radius 1 has circumference 2π.

Comparing reals, including surds, means putting them in decimal form or squaring carefully: to order 2√3 and 3√2, square both (12 vs 18), so 2√3 < 3√2 — valid because both are positive. Beware: for negative numbers squaring reverses the order, so handle signs first. Density: between any two rationals sit infinitely many rationals AND infinitely many irrationals (e.g. add a tiny irrational like 0.010010001… to one endpoint).

A number whose decimal never terminates and never repeats; not a fraction
Any rational or irrational; every point of the number line
A decimal with a repeating block, e.g. 0.1̄8̄ = 0.181818…
Root expressions left exact, e.g. √2, 3√5
Between any two rationals there is another rational (and another irrational)

workedExamples.calculation: √16 = 4 rational; √20 = 2√5 irrational; 22/7 rational (fraction); the pattern decimal never repeats (block grows) → irrational; π irrational

commonMistakes: Calling π '22/7' rational: 22/7 is only an approximation; π itself is irrational
Thinking every decimal is rational — non-repeating patterns like 0.1010010001… are irrational
Believing √2 'must be' 1.41421356: that decimal is a truncation; √2 is the exact diagonal length
Squaring negatives to compare and forgetting to reverse the inequality
Converting 0.3̄ to 3/10 — the recurring trick gives 3/9 = 1/3
applications: Music tuning: repeating rhythms map to recurring decimals; a bar of 3 beats is 1/3 of 9
Construction: diagonal bracing needs √2 — a purely decimal/fraction ruler can never mark it exactly
Finance: interest rates as fractions recur in decimal form (1/3% per day = 1/300)
Computing: floating-point numbers are rationals — the reason 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 exactly in code
g9-mathematics-um2-t1.summary: Numbers nest: ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, with irrationals joining ℚ to complete the line. Rationals are exactly the terminating-or-recurring decimals; convert repeats with the ×10ᵏ − x trick. √2's proof by contradiction shows some lengths defy fractions, and ordering reals means common decimal form (or squaring with sign care).

options: False — integers have no fraction form

questions.explanation: Start with the fraction fully reduced; the algebra then forces both to be even — a contradiction.

questions.explanation: Both sets are dense — averaging gives another rational, and adding a tiny irrational gives one in between.

g9-mathematics-um2-t2.overview: Exponents are a shorthand for repeated multiplication — and the laws that govern them turn monstrous products into single powers. Master scientific notation and you can handle everything from cell sizes to national debt.
objectives: Apply the product, quotient and power laws of exponents
Interpret and compute negative and zero exponents
Write numbers in scientific notation and convert back
Simplify expressions combining several laws
Estimate orders of magnitude with powers of 10
g9-mathematics-um2-t2.simple: aⁿ means 'multiply a by itself n times'. The laws are just bookkeeping: multiplying same-base powers adds the counts (2³·2⁴ = 2⁷); dividing subtracts them (2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³); a power of a power multiplies ( (2³)² = 2⁶). Then the clever bits: a⁰ = 1 (the division law: a³/a³ = a⁰ must be 1) and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ (negative means 'flip to denominator'). Scientific notation just parks one digit before the decimal and counts the shifts as a power of 10.
g9-mathematics-um2-t2.detailed:
For base a and positive integer n, aⁿ is the product of n copies of a. The three laws fall out of counting factors: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (product law), aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (quotient law), (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ (power law). Each extends consistently to all integer exponents — the whole point of defining a⁰ and a⁻ⁿ.

Why a⁰ = 1 (for a ≠ 0): the quotient law demands a³ ÷ a³ = a⁰, but any number divided by itself is 1. Why a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ: again a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³ by the law, but directly it is 1/a³. Consistency, not magic, defines them. Note 0⁰ is left undefined — the two rationales (a⁰=1 vs 0ⁿ=0) clash there.

Scientific notation writes any positive number as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. The exponent counts decimal shifts: 452,000 = 4.52 × 10⁵ (shift 5 left); 0.00083 = 8.3 × 10⁻⁴ (shift 4 right — small numbers get negative exponents). It compresses absurd scales: Ethiopia's population ≈ 1.2 × 10⁸, a red blood cell ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶ m. Multiplying in scientific form is easy: multiply the a-parts, add the exponents: (2×10³)(4×10⁵) = 8×10⁸.

Power-of-a-product and power-of-a-quotient extend the toolkit: (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ and (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ. Simplifying an expression like (2x³)²·x⁻⁴ ÷ x = 2²x⁶·x⁻⁴⁻¹ = 4x requires applying laws in any order that preserves equality — always reduce brackets first, then combine like bases.

Bases that are not the same cannot be combined: 2³ + 2⁴ ≠ 2⁷ (that is 8 + 16 = 24; the product law is for multiplication only). Fractional and negative-base powers get their own care: (−2)⁴ = 16 but −2⁴ = −16 (the exponent applies to 2 first). Orders of magnitude — how many factors of 10 separate two quantities — make quick comparisons: 10⁸ is 100 times bigger than 10⁶.

keyTerms.def: The count of repeated copies of the base: in aⁿ, n is the exponent
aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (same bases, add exponents)

(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ (multiply exponents)
a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0
a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ — moves the factor across the fraction bar
a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10

Finance: compound interest (1 + r)ⁿ is exponential growth in action
Computer science: 2ⁿ memory sizes — a 32 GB phone stores 2³⁵ bytes
Seismology: the Richter scale is base-10 log — one magnitude = ×10 energy
g9-mathematics-um2-t2.summary: Powers are repeated multiplication; the product/quotient/power laws (add, subtract, multiply exponents) extend to zero and negative indices by demanding consistency. Negative exponent = reciprocal, a⁰ = 1, and scientific notation a×10ⁿ (1 ≤ a < 10) compresses huge and tiny magnitudes alike.

g9-mathematics-um2-t3.overview: A radical is just a fraction exponent wearing a hat. Simplify √50 to 5√2, rationalize stubborn denominators, and roots become as easy to handle as powers.
objectives: Convert between radicals and fractional exponents
Simplify surds by extracting perfect-square factors
Add, subtract, multiply and divide surd expressions
Rationalize denominators of the form a/√b and a/(√b ± c)
Estimate irrational roots between consecutive integers
g9-mathematics-um2-t3.simple: √25 asks 'what times itself is 25?' — answer 5. But √50 is not clean: split it into a perfect square × leftovers: √50 = √(25·2) = 5√2. That is 90% of surd work — hunt for square factors. Multiplying surds is easy (√a·√b = √(ab)); adding only works on like surds (2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3, just like x + x). If a fraction has a root downstairs (√2 in the denominator), multiply top and bottom by that root to 'rationalize' it.
g9-mathematics-um2-t3.detailed:
The principal square root √a (a ≥ 0) is the non-negative number whose square is a. Cube roots work for negatives too (∛(−8) = −2). Fractional exponents unify everything: a^(1/2) = √a, a^(1/3) = ∛a, and in general a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ. All the exponent laws now cover roots: a^(1/2)·a^(1/2) = a, which is exactly √a·√a = a.

Simplifying surds means extracting perfect squares: √72 = √(36·2) = 6√2. Always check for square factors 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49… The product and quotient laws make arithmetic light: √a·√b = √(ab) and √a/√b = √(a/b) (a, b ≥ 0, b ≠ 0). Multiplying surds can create simplifiable results: √8·√2 = √16 = 4.

Addition and subtraction need like surds: 3√5 + 7√5 = 10√5, but 3√5 + 2√3 stays as written — you cannot merge different radicands any more than x + y. Mixed problems simplify first, then collect: √12 + √27 = 2√3 + 3√3 = 5√3.

Rationalizing the denominator clears roots from the bottom. For a/√b, multiply by √b/√b: 6/√2 = 6√2/2 = 3√2. For denominators with two terms like √3 + 1, use the conjugate √3 − 1: (√3+1)(√3−1) = 3 − 1 = 2 by the difference-of-squares identity — the surds vanish. So 4/(√3+1) = 4(√3−1)/2 = 2(√3−1).

Estimation keeps irrational roots sane: √50 sits between √49 = 7 and √64 = 8, closer to 7 (≈7.07). On exams, 'between which integers' questions are pure perfect-square bracketing. A final caution: √(a²) = |a|, not a — if a is negative, √(a²) = −a. And √(a+b) ≠ √a + √b (test: √(9+16) = 5 but 3+4 works here by luck; √(4+9) ≈ 3.6 ≠ 2+3). Never distribute a root over addition.

keyTerms.def: The root of a number left in exact form, e.g. √2, ∛5
The expression under the root sign
a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ — roots and powers are one family
Same radicand and index; only these can be added
Clearing radicals from a denominator by multiplying by √b or a conjugate
√a + √b paired with √a − √b; their product a − b has no surds

formulas.name: Radical laws
formulas.meaning: Roots distribute over products and quotients (never sums)

formulas.name: Conjugate product
formulas.meaning: Difference of squares removes the radical

commonMistakes: √(a + b) = √a + √b — roots do NOT distribute over addition
√45 = √(9×5) = 3√5 done wrong as 9√5 — extract the root of the square factor, not the factor itself
Adding unlike surds: 2√3 + 3√2 ≠ 5√5
Forgetting |a| in √(a²): √((−4)²) = 4
Rationalizing with the wrong partner: for √5 − 1 in the denominator, multiply by √5 + 1 (the conjugate), not √5

applications: Geometry: 45-45-90 triangles have legs 1 and hypotenuse √2; equilateral triangle heights use √3
Physics: wave amplitudes and RMS voltages carry √2 factors
Engineering: exact radical answers avoid rounding drift in repeated design calculations
Cryptography: some number-theory schemes live in fields extended by √d
g9-mathematics-um2-t3.summary: Roots are fractional powers: √(ab)=√a√b lets you extract square factors (√50 = 5√2); only like surds add. Multiply surds, then simplify; rationalize single roots with √b/b and two-term denominators with conjugates. √(a²)=|a|, and never split a root over a sum.

g9-mathematics-um2-t4.overview: Logarithms answer the question exponents pose: 'to what power must I raise this base?'. They turn multiplication into addition — the trick that ran engineering slide rules for three centuries.
objectives: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form
Apply the product, quotient and power laws of logs
Use common (log) and natural (ln) logs correctly
Solve simple exponential equations with logs
Evaluate logs from first principles
g9-mathematics-um2-t4.simple: log₂8 = 3 reads: 'the power on 2 that makes 8 is 3'. A log is just an exponent hunted backwards. The laws mirror exponent rules beautifully: multiplying inside a log becomes adding logs; dividing becomes subtracting; a power inside jumps out front as a multiplier. Slide rules worked because log(ab) = log a + log b — turn hard multiplication into easy addition, then look up the answer.
g9-mathematics-um2-t4.detailed:
Definition: log_b x = y ⇔ bʸ = x (b > 0, b ≠ 1, x > 0). The logarithm literally is the exponent. log₁₀ (written 'log') is the common logarithm for base-10 work; logₑ (written 'ln') uses e ≈ 2.718 and dominates science. Two instant identities: log_b 1 = 0 (b⁰ = 1) and log_b b = 1 (b¹ = b).

The three laws inherit from exponent arithmetic. Product: log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y. Quotient: log_b(x/y) = log_b x − log_b y. Power: log_b(xⁿ) = n log_b x. Proof of the product law: let log x = m, log y = n so x = bᵐ, y = bⁿ; then xy = bᵐ⁺ⁿ, hence log(xy) = m + n. Every law is this one-line exponent chase.

Evaluating without tables: log₂32 = 5 because 2⁵ = 32; log₃(1/9) = −2 because 3⁻² = 1/9; log 1000 = 3, ln e⁴ = 4. The number system laws carry over — e.g. log₂(8·4) = log₂8 + log₂4 = 3 + 2 = 5 = log₂32 ✓.

Change of base extends a calculator's buttons: log_b x = log x / log b (any convenient base — use 10 or e). So log₅100 = log 100 / log 5 = 2 / 0.699 ≈ 2.86 — check: 5^2.86 ≈ 100 ✓.

Solving exponential equations: if 2ˣ = 50, take logs: x log 2 = log 50, so x = log 50 / log 2 ≈ 5.64 (between 2⁵ = 32 and 2⁶ = 64, as expected). Domain guardrails: logs of zero or negatives are undefined (no exponent makes bʸ ≤ 0), and the base itself must be positive and ≠ 1. Beware the classic algebra traps: log(x + y) ≠ log x + log y, and log x · log y ≠ log(xy) — the product law is about multiplying the INSIDES, not the logs.

keyTerms.def: log_b x = y means bʸ = x — the log is the exponent
Base 10, written log x
Base e, written ln x
log(xy) = log x + log y
log(xⁿ) = n log x
log_b x = log x ÷ log b

formulas.name: Laws of logarithms

formulas.meaning: Multiply inside → add logs; divide inside → subtract; power inside → out front
formulas.when: Expanding, condensing or evaluating log expressions

formulas.name: Change of base

commonMistakes: log(x + y) = log x + log y — the product law is for MULTIPLYING arguments only
Mixing which side is the base: in log₂8, the 2 is the base; 8 is the argument

Trying log(−5): arguments must be positive

Forgetting 'log' alone means base 10 while 'ln' means base e
applications: Earthquakes: Richter magnitude = log₁₀ of wave amplitude — magnitude 6 is ×10 stronger than 5
Sound: decibels are 10·log of power ratios (20 dB = 100× louder in power)
Finance: doubling time of an investment solves (1+r)ᵗ = 2 with logs — t = log2/log(1+r)
pH scale: acidity = −log₁₀ of hydrogen ion concentration, pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4
g9-mathematics-um2-t4.summary: A logarithm is an exponent viewed from the other side: log_b x = y ⇔ bʸ = x. Products become sums, quotients become differences, powers become multipliers — plus change-of-base for calculators. Solving bˣ = k means x = log k ÷ log b, and arguments must stay positive.

questions.explanation: The log base e undoes the power base e: ln e⁵ = 5.
log_b x = log x ÷ log b.
Only the product law holds; logs never split over sums or differences.
